dxpkirpjls.authorBlurb: I've lived in London for the past 5 years, in a few different areas - and I love it! My favourite things about London are the diversity of people here, the outdoor spaces, and the live music.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.notes:
In this guide, I've honed in on the things I love about London. I've highlighted a few neighbourhoods that could make for a fun afternoon or evening of exploring. Hopefully you'll get a taste not just of why this is a world-famous city, but of what it's like to actually live here!
It should go without saying that this guide is not complete - London is vast, it's hard to pick favourites and I'll be discovering new neighbourhoods and things to do here for years to come! 
Check out these resources for more ideas: 
Events going on right now, things to do: Time Out London, Londonist
Restaurants: Eater London, Halal Food Guy on Instagram
Music: Dice

sections.heading: General tips
sections.notes:
Getting around
Public transportation is very good - albeit expensive - in London, and is usually faster than driving or taking a taxi around. Don't discount walking as an option though as the city is really walkable, with handy maps on many street corners in the central areas to help you navigate.
Public transport in London is largely cashless, so you will need to use a contactless bank card, Apple Pay, Google Pay or an Oyster card to get around. I'd recommend only getting an Oyster if you don't have the other alternatives or if you will be charged a transaction fee on your bank card. 
If you're planning to take several tube journeys a day, there's no need to get a day travel card or similar, as your tube usage will cap out at an amount less than a travel card would cost (see this PDF for this year's caps). A handy feature of London buses is the 'hopper' scheme -- you can make unlimited bus journeys within an hour for the cost of a single journey (currently £1.50). 
Many of us rely on apps to figure out how to get around. Citymapper is a much-loved option with handy features like embedded maps and journey price information, but if you're not inclined to download a new app Google Maps also has excellent coverage.
Late at night your options are the tube, several lines of which run all night on weekends only, night buses, and taxis. Uber is alive and well in London despite an ongoing licensing dispute with the city, but there are also many alternatives which could be cheaper or offering discounts: Bolt, ViaVan, Ola are a few that I've got on my phone. London black taxis are iconic but much more expensive than the other options - use Gett if you're going to get one. 
Money
I hardly ever use cash in London. I don't even really use my bank cards, as Apple Pay and Google Pay are accepted pretty much everywhere. As a tourist, there may be places you go that do require cash, so keep some on you just in case - some street food markets, small cafes and convenience shops may have a minimum spend for card transactions or not take cards all together. 
Connectivity
You'll be able to find WiFi in many cafes (Starbucks is always a good bet) and some shops. If you're in London for a few days, I recommend picking up a SIM card from any supermarket or convenience shop - they all retail for around £1, and a £10 add-on package should get you plenty of data and talk time.

blocks.name: South Bank
blocks.note: I love a stroll along the South Bank. This is a tree-lined riverside walkway going past lots of landmarks, like the National Theatre, the London Eye and the Millennium Bridge. You can easily spend an afternoon taking in sights here. If you're there on a Friday or Saturday, don't miss the South Bank Centre Food Market.

blocks.name: Tate Modern
blocks.note: One of my favourite museums in London, this is a modern art gallery on the South Bank facing the Millennium Bridge. It's in an old power station, and there's always a vast installation in the Turbine Hall that's worth seeing. Like most museums in London, entrance is free!

blocks.name: Trafalgar Square
blocks.note: Another iconic London landmark - also check out the National Gallery and National Portrait Gallery (both free to enter) close by.

sections.notes: These are some of the places you'll find on pretty much every guide to London - so I'd be remiss if I left them out. These are probably all quite touristy and busy, but they're all London landmarks so definitely check out a couple of them at least.

sections.heading: Activities
sections.notes: After a long day of touristing, I need some downtime. Here are some activities around the city that I enjoy. You may have to book at some of these, so check their website or call ahead.

blocks.formatted_address: 176 Prince of Wales Rd, London NW5 3PT, UK
blocks.name: Zabludowicz Collection
blocks.note: Start your Camden exploration with some modern art. The Zabludowicz Collection is in an old Methodist church a short walk from Camden Town - I happened upon it once and found myself engrossed by a contemporary video art exhibition.

blocks.formatted_address: 407 Chalk Farm Rd, Camden Town, London NW1 8AH, UK
blocks.name: Amy Winehouse Statue
blocks.note: This memorial statue of Amy Winehouse is inside the Stables Market, a large market complex on Chalk Farm road.

sections.heading: A Day in Camden Town
sections.notes: Camden Town is a bustling area with plenty of markets, live music venues and places to eat. There's so much to do here, all within walking distance -- it can get a bit hectic at times, but Camden's saving grace is its proximity to the Regents Canal and the parks around, which you can escape to for some peace and quiet.

sections.heading: Islington highlights
sections.notes: Islington is largely a residential area, known for being quite well-heeled and liberal. There are lots of nice things to eat, see and do here. This is a collection of pubs, venues and restaurants that I'd recommend.

sections.heading: Exploring Tooting
sections.notes: A ride on the Northern Line will take you down south to the Tooting. Named one of the world's coolest neighbourhoods by Lonely Planet in 2017, Tooting is multicultural and charming, filled with delicious food; a nice change from the hubbub of central London. It's a bit of a trek from central London, but a good option for an evening of eating and drinking.

sections.heading: Greenwich sights
sections.notes: Greenwich is an area in the East famous as the site of the Greenwich meridian line, where 0 degrees longitude is marked. It's got a lovely park, a few museums, and the Cutty Sark, a 19th century tea clipper ship that's docked on land.

sections.heading: About New York City
sections.notes:
New York, often called New York City (NYC), is the most populous city in the United States. With a 2020 population of 8,804,190 distributed over 300.46 square miles (778.2 km2), New York City is also the most densely populated major city in the United States. Located at the southern tip of New York State, the city is based in the Eastern Time Zone and constitutes the geographical and demographic center of both the Northeast megalopolis and the New York metropolitan area, the largest metropolitan area in the world by urban landmass. With over 20.1 million people in its metropolitan statistical area and 23.5 million in its combined statistical area as of 2020, New York is one of the world's most populous megacities. New York City is a global cultural, financial, and media center with a significant influence on commerce, health care and life sciences, entertainment, research, technology, education, politics, tourism, dining, art, fashion, and sports. New York is the most photographed city in the world. Home to the headquarters of the United Nations, New York is an important center for international diplomacy, an established safe haven for global investors, and is sometimes described as the capital of the world. Wikipedia

WOW! New York City is one of those places that lives up to all of the hype. Our first experience of the Big Apple was amazing, to say the least. What really stands out is the constant hustle and bustle whether in the streets, in Central Park or one of the many attractions of the city. For first time visitors to the city the excitement is almost palpable. I guess, initially, it can be a bit daunting  but it does not take long to get into the mood. One of the most difficult decisions to make when in NYC is what to do and see. There is just so much available and choices can be difficult. Of course there are the "must see" attractions which make a visit to NYC such a wonderful experience.🦔

blocks.note: The Brooklyn Bridge is a hybrid cable-stayed/suspension bridge in New York City, spanning the East River between the boroughs of Manhattan and Brooklyn. Opened on May 24, 1883, the Brooklyn Bridge was the first fixed crossing of the East River. It was also the longest suspension bridge in the world at the time of its opening, with a main span of 1,595.5 feet (486.3 m) and a deck 127 ft (38.7 m) above mean high water. Wikipedia

Nicknamed "The Showplace of the Nation", it is the headquarters for the Rockettes, the precision dance company. Wikipedia

blocks.note: Central Park is an urban park in New York City located between the Upper West and Upper East Sides of Manhattan. It is the fifth-largest park in the city, covering 843 acres (341 ha). It is the most visited urban park in the United States, with an estimated 42 million visitors annually as of 2016, and is the most filmed location in the world. Wikipedia

blocks.name: Teatro La Fenice
blocks.note:
🇬🇧 One of the most renowned and historic opera theaters in Italy and the world. The theater first opened in 1792 and has since been the venue for the greatest opera works. The theater has witnessed numerous premieres of operatic works by composers such as Rossini, Bellini, Donizetti, and Verdi, contributing to its established position in the world of opera. Additionally, Teatro La Fenice is known for its beautiful architecture and unique interior decoration, making it one of the most picturesque opera theaters in the world.
🇵🇱 Najbardziej renomowanych i historycznych teatrów operowych we Włoszech oraz na świecie. Teatr został otwarty po raz pierwszy w 1792 roku i od tego czasu był miejscem, gdzie wystawiane były największe dzieła operowe. Teatr był świadkiem licznych premier operowych dzieł takich kompozytorów jak Rossini, Bellini, Donizetti czy Verdi, co przyczyniło się do jego ugruntowanej pozycji w świecie opery. Ponadto, Teatro La Fenice jest znane z pięknej architektury i wyjątkowego wystroju wnętrza, co sprawia, że jest jednym z najbardziej malowniczych teatrów operowych na świecie.

🇬🇧 Another of Venice's sestieri is Cannaregio, the Jewish quarter. This former ghetto was established in 1516 and still has a strong Jewish population to this day.

Many don't realise that Burano is also important for its embroidery and lace, so expect more souvenir shopping here too!
PS. You will need two hours to visit the place, to eat, to buy souvenirs, to take photos, because it is a very small island.

Wielu nie zdaje sobie sprawy, że Burano jest również ważne ze względu na haft i koronkę, więc spodziewaj się tu również więcej zakupów pamiątek!
PS. Aby zwiedzic to miejsce, zjesc, kupic pamiatki, porobic zdjecia bedziecie potrzebowac dwóch godzin, ponieważ jest to bardzo mała wyspa.

blocks.formatted_address: Campo S. Donato, 11, 30141 Venezia VE, Italy
blocks.name: Basilica dei Santi Maria e Donato
blocks.note:
🇬🇧 Dating from the 7th century, the Basilica of Saint Mary and Saint Donatus is the cathedral on the island of Murano.
Inside, exquisite Byzantine mosaics of Ravenna quality cover the floor and the dome. Outside, the bell tower, like most bell towers, is separate from the church.
While many churches contain the bones of saints, this basilica contains more than just the relics of Saint Donatus. The church of St Donatus. Behind the altar hang four rib bones measuring more than a metre in length.
According to legend, these bones come from a dragon that St Donatus killed in Greece. 
🇵🇱 Pochodząca z VII wieku Bazylika Świętej Marii i Świętego Donata jest katedrą na wyspie Murano.
Wewnątrz wykwintne bizantyjskie mozaiki jakości Rawenny pokrywają podłogę i kopułę. Na zewnątrz dzwonnica, podobnie jak większość dzwonnic, jest oddzielona od kościoła.
Podczas gdy wiele kościołów zawiera kości świętych, ta bazylika zawiera więcej niż tylko relikwie świętego Donata. Kościół św. Donata. Za ołtarzem wiszą cztery kości żebrowe mierzące ponad metr długości.
Według legendy kości te pochodzą od smoka, którego św. Donat zabił w Grecji. .

blocks.formatted_address: Campo Santo Stefano, 30124 Venezia VE, Italy
blocks.name: Campo Santo Stefano
blocks.note:
🇬🇧 Campo Santo Stefano is best known for Simone Cenedese's 'Comet Glass Star', an abstract blue glass sculpture in the middle of the square.
Juxtaposed with historic buildings and rich culture, this modern artefact reflects Murano's deep-rooted glassmaking tradition, while showing its evolution.
Next to it is the Church of St Stephen and the 19th-century clock tower. Both dominate the island and are visible from a distance.
🇵🇱 Campo Santo Stefano jest najbardziej znane z "Comet Glass Star" Simone Cenedese, abstrakcyjnej niebieskiej szklanej rzeźby pośrodku placu.
Zestawiony z historycznymi budynkami i bogatą kulturą, ten nowoczesny artefakt odzwierciedla głęboko zakorzenioną tradycję szklarską Murano, jednocześnie pokazując jej ewolucję.
Obok znajduje się kościół św. Stefana i XIX-wieczna wieża zegarowa. Oba dominują nad wyspą i są widoczne z daleka.

blocks.formatted_address: Fondamenta da Mula, 152, 30141 Venezia VE, Italy
blocks.name: Palazzo da Mula
blocks.note:
🇬🇧 Palazzo da Mula is one of the last surviving examples of Venetian Gothic architecture built around the 15th or 16th century.
The building was once the luxurious summer residence of Venetian patricians, who could afford an ornate façade with large Gothic windows.
The exterior of the building still has the beautiful features of the Venetian Gothic style, with reddish bricks and an elegant tiled roof. 
🇵🇱 Palazzo da Mula jest jednym z ostatnich zachowanych przykładów weneckiej architektury gotyckiej zbudowanej około XV lub XVI wieku.

pgcjjrdlqk.authorBlurb: Visited Barcelona with my family. These are the spots we discovered and recommendations from locals. If you found this guide helpful, please like & follow me to see more destinations.

sections.heading: General tips
sections.notes:
Plan Ahead: Book tickets for popular attractions in advance.
Watch for Pickpockets: Keep belongings secure, especially in crowded areas. Not unlike any other major city. 
Explore Neighborhoods: Each has its own vibe. 
Try Local Cuisine: Sample tapas, seafood, and visit La Boqueria market.
Respect Customs: Dress appropriately for religious sites. 
Embrace the Culture: Enjoy the vibrant street life, festivals, and nightlife.

blocks.name: Gràcia
blocks.note:
Coolest neighborhood
A former standalone municipality, Barcelona has long since swallowed Gràcia whole – and it then had the gall to become the city's coolest district. With local design workshops, vegan restaurants, and even Japanese patisseries, the neighborhood is a tick-list of trendy spots.
Besides the organic food stores and yoga studios, there's plenty of traditional Catalan culture here too. Not least the language and the popular events that regularly take place in the neighborhood. In the daytime, Gràcia's squares fill with market stalls which are then removed in the evening as locals gather for drinks from 7pm.
Packed with all types of restaurants, from local tapas joints to Michelin-star restaurants, Gràcia is also a great neighborhood for strolling, bar-hopping, and soaking in the atmosphere. You can also find architectural gems here designed by Modernist architect Antoni Gaudí. Seek out Casa Vicens and Park Güell. Well-connected with downtown, Gràcia is ideal for those wanting to be close to the city center without being part of the hustle and bustle.

blocks.name: La Barceloneta
blocks.note:
Best neighborhood for beaches 
A year-round vacation spot, Barceloneta("Little Barcelona") is the preferred neighborhood for tourists thanks to its glorious necklace of beaches. Originally a traditional fishing district founded in the 18th century, Barceloneta later became a working-class area as industrial expansion around the city harbor grew. You still get a sense of the industrial roots as you stroll along the historic narrow lanes here.
While the area's buildings lack the patrician facades that characterize other parts of Barcelona, they have kept their own unique character and today house a wide array of tapas bars and nightclubs. Though most stay in Barceloneta for late-night parties or beach action, Barceloneta has plenty of spots for families to enjoy. Stroll around Port Vell (Old Harbor) and along the animated promenade. Kids will also like L’Aquàrium and the Museu d’Història de Catalunya.

blocks.name: El Born
blocks.note:
Best neighborhood for sightseeing. 
El Born competes with Gràcia for the title of Barcelona's trendiest neighborhood, but instead of vegan restaurants and urban gardens, El Born is home to concept stores, art studios and a distinctly international vibe. Formerly a crafts district, El Born is one of the oldest neighborhoods in Barcelona and you can browse the many independent art galleries and boutiques for free. Look for century-old shops such as Casa Perris (a grocery store that sells in bulk) and some of the most important landmarks in the city, including Basílica de Santa Maria del Mar, a Gothic church from the 14th century, and Palau de la Música, a music hall and one of the best examples of Modernist architecture.
If your budget allows, El Born has a wide range of fine-dining restaurants, mostly offering Mediterranean and Spanish cuisine. For those on a budget, you can also find plenty of international fast-food eateries and an endless supply of bars. El Born enjoys a prime location between Barceloneta and the city center and is within walking distance of most city landmarks, making it one of the most popular neighborhoods for accommodations.

blocks.formatted_address: C/ de Mallorca, 401, L'Eixample, 08013 Barcelona, Spain
blocks.name: La Sagrada Familia
blocks.note: The Sagrada Familia in Barcelona is an awe-inspiring masterpiece of Antoni Gaudí, a renowned Catalan architect. This basilica stands as an iconic symbol of Barcelona's skyline, blending Gothic and Art Nouveau styles with its intricate facades and towering spires, perhaps most famous for being under construction since 1882. Visitors marvel at its surrealistic design, vibrant stained glass windows, and organic forms inspired by nature. Make reservations in advance to visit the Cathedral and towers.

blocks.formatted_address: Pla de la Seu, s/n, Ciutat Vella, 08002 Barcelona, Spain
blocks.name: Cathedral of Barcelona
blocks.note:
The Cathedral of Barcelona, officially known as the Cathedral of the Holy Cross and Saint Eulalia, is a majestic Gothic masterpiece nestled in the heart of Barcelona's Gothic Quarter. Dating back to the 13th century, this cathedral showcases stunning architecture with its soaring spires, intricate gargoyles, and a magnificent cloister adorned with lush gardens and palm trees. Inside, visitors discover a serene ambiance with beautifully carved choir stalls, a stunning Gothic altarpiece, and the crypt of Saint Eulalia, the patron saint of Barcelona. The cathedral's rooftop offers panoramic views of the city, making it a must-visit for history enthusiasts and architecture aficionados alike. 
Note: you must have your shoulders covered to enter the cathedral. Shawls are sold by vendors outside.

blocks.formatted_address: Pg. de Gràcia, 43, L'Eixample, 08007 Barcelona, Spain
blocks.name: Casa Batlló
blocks.note: Casa Batlló, a masterpiece of modernist architecture by Antoni Gaudí, stands as a highlight of Barcelona's Passeig de Gràcia. Its distinctive façade, adorned with colorful ceramic tiles and undulating shapes, captivates visitors from around the globe. Inside, Gaudí's creativity shines with organic forms, whimsical details, and innovative use of light and space. From the sweeping staircase to the enchanting rooftop terrace resembling a dragon's back, every corner of Casa Batlló tells a story of Catalan artistry and Gaudí's genius. It's a must-see for those seeking to explore Barcelona's rich architectural heritage and artistic innovation.

blocks.formatted_address: C. de Villarroel, 163, L'Eixample, 08036 Barcelona, Spain
blocks.name: Disfrutar
blocks.note:
L’Eixample, Catalonian
Despite being named the “World’s Best Restaurant 2024”, you’d struggle to find a fine-dining spot more laid-back and actually pleasant than Disfrutar. The three owners were each previously head chefs at elBulli (the place where they started putting foam on plates), and they’ve brought all that expertise here, without any snobbishness. What you see on your plate during one of the tasting menu experiences is rarely what you taste in your mouth, whether that’s a panchino (or bao bun) filled with beluga caviar or a “gazpacho sandwich” that’s actually just sliced bread filled with tomato-flavored meringue and a refreshing gazpacho sorbet.

blocks.formatted_address: C/ de Calvet, 28, Sarrià-Sant Gervasi, 08021 Barcelona, Spain
blocks.name: Colmado Wilmot
blocks.note:
Sarría-Sant Gervasi, Catalonian
When you’ve had it with the dry ice and foam and want to see how real locals eat, go to Colmado Wilmot. This small tapas bar, deli, and grocery store in Sarrià-Sant Gervasi is busy and boisterous—you’re greeted by loud chatter and clinking glasses (they have an impressive wine list), and walls are full of shelves stacked with jars, bottles, and tins. This place does things the way they used to be done, which means great produce, friendly service, and not a squiggle of balsamic glaze or a decorative flower in sight. The menu is full of seafood, bought fresh from the market, like red Mediterranean prawns and plump baby scallops served mostly naked (lightly grilled with a pinch of garlic and salt). Catalunya is set between the mountains and the sea, and dishes reflect that, like the fricandó, a beef stew, with sea cucumber that has depth of flavor.

zlcocpeivp.authorBlurb: Brandon lives in London and is a frequent visitor to Rome. Over the years he has filled many sketchbooks with drawings and paintings of the city.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.notes: Borromini, Baroque, Basilica... Pizza, Piazza, Pantheon... A week-long visit to Rome can be feel like one big blur of new vocabulary words. There are too many architects and periods and styles to remember. How to make sense of it all? In this guide I'll try to connect together different buildings with some of the "big picture" ideas so that you can appreciate the magic of the world's most beautiful city.

sections.heading: Tips
sections.notes: Let Go. Unless you're staying for a week or longer, don't try to see all of the landmarks on your first trip. You could spend your entire trip queuing, stuck in crowds, exhausted. Instead enjoy the atmosphere of the city. Try to understand what makes the city special, rather than just going to the landmarks.Use a Sketchbook. The best way to appreciate Rome is to draw it. The point is not to make a pretty picture. It is to train your eye to notice details you wouldn't have paid attention to otherwise.Look familiar? Ideas about what buildings should look like have traveled from Rome to all corners of the world for millennia. That means that in your home town there are almost certainly buildings that are inspired by–or likely straight up copies of–buildings in Rome. Thus one of the easiest ways to appreciate the architecture of Rome is to think of buildings that you know well and find the buildings in Rome that inspired them.

blocks.formatted_address: Trastevere, Rome, Metropolitan City of Rome, Italy
blocks.name: Trastevere
blocks.note:
For this walk, begin by leaving behind the banks of the River Tiber to explore the leafy bohemian neighborhood of Trastevere. The narrow medieval streets are incredibly picturesque.
Work your way to the western corner of the neighborhood. There are steps starting at Vicolo della Frustra that lead you up the hill...

blocks.formatted_address: Piazza di S. Pietro in Montorio, 3, 00153 Roma RM, Italy
blocks.name: Tempietto del Bramante
blocks.note:
Halfway up the Janiculum, as you're beginning to lose your breath, spare a thought for someone who experienced even more discomfort on the Hill than you: Saint Paul. He was crucified here in 64AD.
At the top of the steps up from the Trastevere is an old church called San Pietro in Montorio. Tucked away inside of a quiet courtyard, on the exact spot of Paul's crucifixion, lives perhaps the loveliest building of the entire Renaissance: the Tempietto by Bramante.
Normally when we have a profound connection with a building, it's because we are standing inside of it. The Tempietto is different. It it is so small that you will feel an intense connection to the building by just standing next to it. There is something incredibly pleasing about its proportions.

blocks.formatted_address: Piazzale Giuseppe Garibaldi, 00165 Roma RM, Italy
blocks.name: Janiculum Terrace
blocks.note:
This is the finest view of Rome.
Looking to the right (east) provides a divine view of central Rome. If you go over to the left (west) side you can see St Peter's and the Vatican.
We can learn a lot about a place by its skyline. Urban designer Ed Bacon wrote "Throughout history, architects have lavished much of their tenderest care on the part of the building which meets the sky. This area has been a characteristic expression of the spirit of the times. Now, all too often, all thought ceases before the sky is reached. We sweep our rubbish into the upper air and use it as the crowning feature of our designs, with pipes, air conditioners, and TV aerials as symbols of our relationship with the infinity of space." Thus to see Rome from above is in a way to be transported into another time. There are few cities left in the world with such an undisturbed skyline. The view you're seeing has been largely the same for centuries. 
Legend has it that the city and the Vatican have a pact: no building can rise above the 136m height of the dome of St Peter's Basilica. Many assume that this rule is encoded in the Lateran Pacts of 1929 that recognized the Vatican as an independent state. When developers announced in 2010 that they were going to build a skyscraper in Rome (five miles as the crow flies from the Janiculum Terrace) there was an uproar. Yet scholars at the Vatican revealed there was no such written agreement. Social pressure alone prevents buildings from destroying the beautiful skyline!
From above, it is easy to grasp Rome as a cohesive whole. Almost everything you see on the east side was part of the ancient city. At its peak, one million Romans lived inside the Aurelian walls of Rome. The city spanned 5.4 square miles in size. For comparison, at the same time Londinium (which would later become London) was just 0.5 square miles. It was only in the nineteenth century that another city—London—was as massive as ancient Rome.

sections.heading: Day 1: Rome from Above
sections.notes: The best way to begin your experience of Rome is to see it from above. Atop the Janiculum Hill the noise of the city fades away and hundreds of towers, domes, and spires stretch to the horizon.

blocks.formatted_address: Via la Spezia, 3, 00182 Roma RM, Italy
blocks.name: Stazione San Giovanni Metro C
blocks.note: The Metro C train line was recently extended further into the city. As the digging proceeded, archaeologists discovered hundreds of artifacts. Not only are these artifacts now on display in the station...the walls are covered with giant infographics that show you the layers of Roman history. In the lobby level are artifacts from the modern age. But as you descend down the steps you can feel yourself going back in time...to the medieval age, the imperial age, and finally, standing on the train platform at an elevation of -26m, to an age before humans had even arrived.

blocks.name: St. Clement Basilica
blocks.note:
The church of San Clemente is the most dramatic example of the buried world beneath Rome. At ground level there is a fantastic 12th century basilica. But in the 19th century, Romans discovered that buried beneath the church was a Byzantine chapel from the 4th century. And then later still they discovered that there is a Roman Mythraen temple even further down.
When you visit you can go down down down underground and find yourself walking along the remains of a Roman street, peeping into the Mythraen temple to your left and the Royal Mint to your right. There, deep underground, you can stop for a moment and imagine how many splendors lie forever buried beneath Rome!

blocks.formatted_address: Via della Domus Aurea, 1, 00184 Roma RM, Italy
blocks.name: Domus Aurea
blocks.note:
Imagine it's 1480. Everyday life is stressful. So you decide to go on a walk with your friend through the parkland on the Palatine Hill--the mythical place where Romulus and Remus founded the city milennia ago. So. You're walking along, relaxed, glad to have a bit of escape from the madness of your life. Then...you hear a scream and a loud thud. Your friend has disappeared into a hole in the ground.
This is exactly what happened in ~1480AD. When a lantern was lowered down into the hole, the stunned Romans discovered that the space he had fallen into was not just an ordinary cave. It was a vaulted ceiling covered in colorful Roman frescoes. 
Everyone knows that Emperor Nero twiddled his thumbs while Rome burned in 64AD. But what the fifteenth century Romans discovered was that Nero was also a firm believer in the practice of Carpe Diem...for he built himself a massive palace—the Domus Aurea—on top of the charred remains of the mansions that had previously occupied the Palatine Hill. 
Within a few years Nero was dead. Romans were keen to forget about him. Within a decade the palace had been buried in dirt, and new buildings were constructed on top of it. Nero's loss is our gain. This practice of burying has left the villa well preserved to this day. Explore it!

sections.heading: Rome from Below
sections.notes:
When you are walking in central Rome, you are not just walking on dirt. At any given time you are most likely walking on one, two or maybe even three ancient structures dating back thousands of years...entombed beneath the Eternal City.
Why is this the case? In old times when locals needed a new building they would fill the remains of the old with earth, and then use this dirt-embalmed building as a foundation. 
The most mind-boggling part? We will probably never know what is buried beneath most of Rome. To get a taste of what secrets are hidden in this parallel world, we must descend into the depths of massive construction projects like the Metro, or retrace the steps unlucky Romans who have fallen into mysterious holes...

blocks.formatted_address: Via del Quirinale, 23, 00187 Roma RM, Italy
blocks.name: Chiesa di San Carlino alle Quattro Fontane
blocks.note: This is one of the first great works of Baroque architecture (finished in 1646). The break with the classical design system is visible even from the street. Gone are the flat facade and right angles that had defined buildings since the start. Instead Borromini set off to build a new system of order where curves, ellipses and intricacy are brought together into a harmonious whole. The undulating facade gets your attention, and the new ideas are carried to the logical extreme within, where interlocking ellipses and a cascade of trapezoids, hexagons, octagons, and crosses combine to gesture towards Heaven.

blocks.formatted_address: Corso del Rinascimento, 40, 00186 Roma RM, Italy
blocks.name: St. Ivo alla Sapienza
blocks.note: Only open on Sunday mornings for one hour. Plan your trip around it. It is worth it. To unlock its geometric secrets bring a pen and paper. Sit down and draw the floor plan. If you’re able, draw the plan of the rooftop right above the plan of the floor. See the pattern? Everything you see around you is designed to help fit these two shapes together. That is the beauty of this design: the simple mathematical ideas that have been used to generate order.

sections.heading: Borromini's Baroque Masterpieces
sections.notes:
There are a lot of churches in Rome. That's a fact. I've only included two in this guide because I think it's important that you see the "essence" of the Baroque movement.
At the time of the Protestant Reformation, architects in Rome had inherited a long, ancient tradition of classical architecture. They were adept at using building blocks like columns, friezes, pediments and vaults to create beauty. Words that spring to mind to describe structures like this include "sober" and "elegant". But this was not enough for the Catholic Church. The rise of the protestants made the Church nervous. So they began patronizing new architects to develop a new, more emotional style of buildings that would strike awe into the hearts of visitors. 
The result was the Baroque movement. Roman architects like Bernini and Borromini not only had to change the emotional experience of going to church. They had to develop an entirely new way of packing complexity into a building--both the interior and the facade--while somehow making it still look harmonious and beautiful.

sections.heading: Piazzas
sections.notes:
The most dramatic moments in Rome arrive not when looking at a building, but by moving in the grand spaces between buildings: piazzas. When you move through the piazzas of Rome pay attention to…
The way buildings meet the skyThe way key points move in space as you moveThe way different depths are visible in the same viewThe curvature of the spacesThe way you ascend and descend through spaceIf you train your eyes to take in all of these details the result is architectural overstimulation at its best.

sections.heading: Rome, Fallen.
sections.notes:
When you visit the monuments of Ancient Rome your first reaction will probably be: "Isn't it amazing that all of this survived!" O historical preservation! O progress! What riches are ours.
Yet in the centuries after the Renaissance, tourists had the opposite reaction as they surveyed the ruins of empire: "My God. How far Rome has fallen!"
The first tourists were young English gentlemen in the 1700s. As students, they were raised on a steady diet of Latin, Cicero, and Virgil. The wealthiest were sent on a Grand Tour to complete their education. As Roger Hudson put it, for parents, "the Classical heritage was Civilization, for all intents and purposes, and they sought to give their child at worst a thin coating, at best a thorough marinading, by immersing him at its fount." 
What they found when they arrived in Rome came as a tremendous shock. To visit Rome in that time was to come face to face with nothing short of the collapse of Civilization. Ruins as far as the eye could see. Overgrown with plants. The Rome that greeted them was very different than the one you will see. But with a bit of imagination, you, too can be moved by the magnitude of historical change.

znordifcrv.authorBlurb: After my amazing experience at the land of ice and fire with 2 friends, I decided to share my itinerary for fellow travelers. I travelled to Iceland at September of 2024, so this itinerary is for September trips!

sections.heading: General tips
sections.notes:
At the beginning let’s state some general tips:
1. Time of the year: As we travelled at September I have to say that I think it’s one of the best seasons to visit Iceland. Main reasons are:
Weather is not so bad as the rest of autumn and winter (less weather alerts)Prices are a lot lower than summer (shoulder season).Crowds are also more rare than summer.Some f-roads that lead to the majestic highlands are still open (more possibly at the beginning of September)You can see aurora borealis (it’s dark enough at night and it has good activity)You have enough daylight hours to visit enough spots (sunrise around 6am and sunset around 8pm)The landscapes are coloured with the characteristic vibrant green colour and are amazing!
2. Transportation: If you want to do the ring road at your own pace (without guides) you’ll have to rent a vehicle. The main options are three:
Small 2wd car: the cheaper option. At September it is possible but you’ll miss many spots that require bigger cars due to rough roads (and the highlands that have f-roads)4wd car: That’s what I chose. medium cost option. There are many types and sizes of 4wd cars and you can choose the one that matches your itinerary ( the 4wd cars can enter the f-roads and the highlands)Campervan: it combines transportation with lodging and its a good option at that time of the year. You may have some problems if strong winds are forecasted (wind-sensitive vehicle)
3. Lodging: in order to circle the whole country you’ll need many different accommodations. We stayed at 7 different places around the country. We used Airbnb and booking to make the reservations. The small wooden houses in the middle of nowhere were a highlight of the trip! Two of them had also a jacuzzi. The prices with enough research and early booking will be good.
4. Itinerary: Everyone online will suggest to not overpack your itinerary and give time to each stop. I will tell you to plan according your pace and your type of vacations you want to do! You want to chill out and visit 2-3 main landscapes each day? That’s fine! You want to get tired, wake early and be on a little rush to visit many things? That’s also fine! We were on the second category and didn’t regret it at all! So this itinerary will be a little overpacked, with early wake times. If it doesn’t work for you you can skip some places! Also you should be flexible to change your travel plans according to weather!
!! Note that driving times will be a lot in this itinerary so sharing the wheel is necessary !! By

blocks.name: Keflavík International Airport
blocks.note: We arrived at the airport at 1:20 pm and went to pick up our car. Rental companies are really organized and we had our car ready at 2:30 pm

blocks.name: Just Wingin It
blocks.note:
Quick stop for food. Really tasty chicken fingers but a little bit expensive (get used to it in Iceland!). We also did our first supermarket shopping for our trip. 
Rate 3/5

blocks.name: Dead Man Walk
blocks.note:
Part of Thingvellir National park. we decided to park at P3 and visit this site first, then to head at P2 to see the rest of the park. This is a quick way to see everything the park has to offer! 
If you visit the park don’t skip this area! It’s also a must for GOT fans. 
Rate 4/5

blocks.name: Hjálparfoss
blocks.note:
First waterfall of the many to come for that day! Very nice warm up for the ones to come. The surroundings was nice too with some basalt columns. Tip: very nice photos opportunity in front of the waterfall. 
Rate 3/5

blocks.name: Sigoldufoss
blocks.note:
First stop of the day. Waterfall with very blue waters and with vivid green coloured surrounding mountains. A nice quick stop on our way. 
Rate 4/5

blocks.name: Mossy Lava Fields
blocks.note:
On this site you can see from the road these mossy lava fields as far as the eye can see. You can park at a parking on the right side and walk a small path into the mossy fields. Also there is a small road for more adventure driving into this scenery. I recommend the stop at the parking. Tip: never step on the moss! It took millions of years to grow. 
Rate 4/5

blocks.name: Folaldafoss
blocks.note:
We had planned to head to the Eastfjords through road 939 (also named oxi). This road was one of the best we drove on our trip, with mountains all around and little rivers and waterfalls on the way (if you’re afraid of heights I don’t suggest it). This site was a parking on the side of the road with perfect view where we ate our breakfast. If you want you can go as close to the waterfall you like! 
Rate 3/5

blocks.name: Rjúkandi Waterfall
blocks.note:
Another road-side waterfall. You can either take photos from the car (that’s what we did) or stop and go as close as you want if you have time. It’s not something special compared to what you have already seen 
Rate 2/5
